name: Mattapan
headline: The trolley's last stop at Mattapan Square,
triple-deckers, a nature sanctuary and the Neponset trail.
answer: Mattapan is a neighborhood in southern Boston, part of the town of Dorchester when Boston annexed it in 1870, centered on Mattapan Square, where Blue Hill Avenue, River Street and Cummins Highway meet. Its housing includes triple-deckers, two-family and single-family houses and small apartment buildings, and the Boston Planning & Development Agency counted 23,834 people there in 2020. The Mattapan Line trolley ends at Mattapan station, and the Fairmount Line stops at Morton Street and Blue Hill Avenue.
meta: Mattapan, Boston: triple-deckers and two-family houses around Mattapan Square, with the Mattapan Line trolley, two Fairmount Line stops and the Neponset trail.

boundaries.text: Mattapan is in the south of Boston, centered on Mattapan Square at the meeting of Blue Hill Avenue, River Street and Cummins Highway. Harambee Park in Dorchester's Franklin Field lies beside it, and the Boston Nature Center and Forest Hills Cemetery, in the adjoining Forest Hills area, are sometimes counted as its green space.

overview: Mattapan takes its name from the Massachusett name for the Dorchester area, recorded as 'Matampan' in 1634. Paths that became Adams Street and River Street led to fishing weirs at Lower Mills, and Mattapan and Lower Mills were the main fords of the Neponset River. On December 1, 1847, the Dorchester and Milton Branch Railroad began service to a station at Upper Mills that was later renamed Mattapan, and on December 18, 1849, the Mattapan Library Association opened. Mattapan was part of Dorchester when Boston annexed that town in 1870, and it grew in the late 19th and early 20th centuries as railroads and streetcars brought downtown within reach. The present Mattapan station building opened on July 4, 1902, after Blue Hill Avenue was widened.

In 1929 the Milton branch railroad became the Mattapan Line, a trolley that opened from Ashmont to Milton on August 26 and on to Mattapan on December 21; it runs beside the Neponset River and still uses PCC streetcars built in 1945 and 1946. The housing that filled in around the square is mostly wood-frame: triple-deckers, two-family and single-family houses, with small apartment buildings on River Street. To the north, the city's Boston State Hospital, which spread across land in Mattapan and Dorchester from 1887, closed in 1979; part of the grounds became Mass Audubon's Boston Nature Center, and 40 acres were redeveloped as Olmsted Green, 497 homes built in phases over 18 years, the last of them sold by February 2026.

The Fairmount Line's Morton Street station, a stop since the line's early days, reopened in 1979 and was rebuilt with accessible platforms in 2007, and a new station at Blue Hill Avenue and Woodhaven Street opened on February 25, 2019. In April 2023 The Loop at Mattapan Station opened on the station's former parking lot, with 135 rental apartments and ground-floor retail. The Boston Planning & Development Agency board adopted PLAN: Mattapan on May 11, 2023; residential zoning allowing two- and three-unit infill and accessory dwelling units followed on February 7, 2024, and on May 30, 2024 Mattapan Square became the first place in the city mapped with Squares + Streets zoning, which allows mixed-use buildings and multifamily housing.

housing.text: The Boston Planning Department describes Mattapan's housing as modest multi-unit buildings, detached single-family houses, public housing and traditional triple-deckers; two- and three-family houses are common, and apartment buildings line parts of River Street. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 9,214 occupied housing units in Mattapan, 40.4% of them owner-occupied, compared with 35.3% citywide.

areas.name: Mattapan Square
areas.line: The commercial center where Blue Hill Avenue, River Street and Cummins Highway meet, with Mattapan station at River Street and Blue Hill Avenue, the end of the trolley line and of eight bus routes; it was the first area mapped with Squares + Streets zoning, in 2024.

areas.name: Blue Hill Avenue
areas.line: With Mattapan Square, the neighborhood's main commercial street, with the Mattapan Branch Library at number 1350 and the Fairmount Line's Blue Hill Avenue station at Woodhaven Street.

areas.name: Former Boston State Hospital grounds
areas.line: The old hospital campus, closed in 1979, now divided between the 67-acre Boston Nature Center on Walk Hill Street and Olmsted Green, a 40-acre development of 497 homes, 80% of them deed-restricted affordable and 28% for ownership.

areas.name: Morton Street
areas.line: The corridor around Morton Street station at 865 Morton Street, a Fairmount Line stop between Talbot Avenue and Blue Hill Avenue.

rail.line: Mattapan Line (trolley, part of the Red Line)

commute.text: The Mattapan Line trolley runs about 2.5 miles from Mattapan station along the Neponset River to Ashmont, where it meets the Red Line. The Fairmount Line stops at Morton Street and Blue Hill Avenue on its way between Readville and South Station, through Dorchester. Eight MBTA bus routes end at Mattapan station, and Blue Hill Avenue, River Street, Cummins Highway and Morton Street are the main roads.

places.name: Boston Nature Center and Wildlife Sanctuary
places.line: Mass Audubon's 67-acre sanctuary at 500 Walk Hill Street, with gardens, meadows, woods and wetlands; admission is free, and part of the land was once Boston State Hospital.

places.name: Neponset River Greenway
places.line: A paved trail of about nine miles through Readville, Hyde Park, Mattapan and Dorchester and into Milton; a 1.3-mile section opened in May 2017 between the Mattapan and Central Avenue trolley stations, linking Mattapan Square to the trail toward Pope John Paul II Park.

places.name: Franklin Park
places.line: Olmsted's park of roughly 485 acres, designed in the 1890s and Boston's largest open space, with the Franklin Park Zoo, the William Devine Golf Course and White Stadium; it connects Mattapan with Roxbury, Dorchester, Jamaica Plain and Roslindale.

places.name: Harambee Park
places.line: A park built in 1898 to a Frederick Law Olmsted design and originally called Franklin Field, in Dorchester beside Mattapan.

places.name: Mattahunt Woods
places.line: A city Urban Wild at 206 Colorado Street, cared for with the Friends of Mattahunt Woods, the Trustees and Boston Parks and Recreation.

places.name: Mattapan Branch Library
places.line: A Boston Public Library branch at 1350 Blue Hill Avenue, opened in February 2009; its history goes back to the Mattapan Library Association of 1849.

history.text: The Dorchester and Milton Branch Railroad began service on December 1 to a station at Upper Mills, later renamed Mattapan.
Boston annexed the town of Dorchester, which included Mattapan.
The branch railroad was converted to the Mattapan Line trolley, which reached Mattapan on December 21.
Squares + Streets zoning was encoded for Mattapan Square on May 30, the first area in the city to be mapped, following PLAN: Mattapan, adopted May 11, 2023.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Mattapan?
faq.a: According to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town table, which lists Mattapan on its own row, the median single-family sale price for calendar year 2025 was $627,500, across 34 sales, against $599,950 across 48 sales in 2024. The condominium median was $420,000 in 2025, across 94 sales, against $417,450 across 34 sales in 2024. Two- and three-family houses, common in Mattapan, are not covered by either figure.

Yes. The Fairmount Line stops at Morton Street and at Blue Hill Avenue, which opened in 2019, on its way between Readville and South Station. The Mattapan Line trolley also runs from Mattapan station to Ashmont, where it meets the Red Line.
Boston Public Schools. School assignment is set by the district; review its profile with DESE.

The Mattapan Line, opened in 1929 on a former branch railroad, is a 2.5-mile streetcar line with eight stations between Ashmont and Mattapan that follows the Neponset River and uses PCC streetcars built in 1945 and 1946. The MBTA's Mattapan Line Transformation project plans to replace them with newer light rail vehicles and rebuild the stations.

faq.q: What is Squares + Streets zoning in Mattapan Square?
faq.a: It is a set of Boston zoning districts, adopted in April 2024, that allow mixed-use buildings and multifamily housing in neighborhood centers near transit. Mattapan Square was the first place mapped with it, on May 30, 2024, following PLAN: Mattapan, which the Boston Planning & Development Agency board adopted on May 11, 2023.

notes: Written 2026-10-23. Housing tenure from the same report's Housing Tenure table (ACS 2016-2020): 'Mattapan 9,214 92.0% 3,725 40.4% 5,489 59.6%'; Boston 35.3%. Boundaries: no source gave street boundaries for Mattapan (Wikipedia, the city's neighborhood page and the Planning Department page were checked); the boundaries text uses only the square's location and Wikipedia's notes on adjoining green space. The Wikipedia Mattapan Square article and the Neponset River Greenway article would not load. History: name origin, 'Matampan' (1634), the Adams and River Street paths and the fords, the 1849 library association and the 1870 annexation (infobox date October 7, 1870, not used) from Wikipedia's Mattapan article; railroad of December 1, 1847, Upper Mills renaming, the July 4, 1902 station building, the 2006-2007 rebuild, the eight bus routes (24, 28, 29, 30, 31, 33, 245, 716) and The Loop (April 2023, 135 rental units) from Wikipedia's Mattapan station article; the station's address (500 River St) from mbta.com. Mattapan Line dates, length (2.54 miles in the infobox, 2.6 in the text; given as about 2.5), eight stations, PCC cars and the Transformation project from Wikipedia's Mattapan Line article; only Mattapan station is listed as in the neighborhood (the locations of Capen Street and Valley Road stations were not confirmed). Fairmount stops from the mbta.com timetable; Morton Street station (865 Morton Street, Mattapan; 1855 Forest Avenue stop, 1979 reopening, 2007 rebuild) and Blue Hill Avenue station (Blue Hill Avenue at Woodhaven Street, Mattapan; opened February 25, 2019) from their Wikipedia articles. Boston State Hospital (1887 expansion to Austin Farm, closed 1979, in Mattapan and Dorchester) from Wikipedia; Olmsted Green (40 acres, 497 units, 80% affordable, 28% ownership, 18 years, The Preserve sold out by February 2026) from mass.gov; the Olmsted Green street location was not given. Boston Nature Center facts from Mass Audubon (67 acres, 500 Walk Hill Street, free); the hospital link from Wikipedia. Highways: named as streets only; route numbers were not confirmed. Forest Hills Cemetery is mentioned only as Wikipedia frames it (in Forest Hills, sometimes counted as Mattapan green space). Market: both rows copied from tools/data/boston-neighborhood-rows-2025.json (read 2026-10-23 with pdf.js; YTD lines are calendar years 2024 and 2025); the PDF was not re-read here. The condo count rose from 34 to 94; no reason is given in the source and none is suggested. Schools: assignment is by address and set by Boston Public Schools; no school is named. Nearby: Dorchester (Harambee Park, Cedar Grove and the Mattapan Line), Hyde Park and Roslindale (the Neponset Greenway and Franklin Park pages) and Roxbury (Franklin Park); exact shared borders were not confirmed. Region: kept as 'Greater Boston (the city)' to match the eight existing Boston neighborhood records. Fair housing: Wikipedia's Mattapan article has extensive demographic, immigration, language, income and crime content and an account of 1960s and 1970s population change, blockbusting and redlining told through who moved in and out; none of it is used, even as history. The Planning Department page's name gloss ('a good place to be') and its language list are not used. The Mattapan Community Health Center was left out because its source describes it by the people it serves. The Blue Hill Avenue station's design history (neighbor objections) is left out. No area is characterized by who lives there, and no crime or safety language is used.
